newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China soybean, meal defaults seen continuing - trade.
newsitem.headline: China soybean, meal defaults seen continuing - trade.

text.p: Defaults by Chinese buyers on cargoes of soymeal and soybean already purchased were expected to continue as China had possibly overbought both commodites, grains and oilseeds traders said on Wednesday.
No estimates were available for how much China may have overbought.
"The problem now is willingness of buyers to accept cargoes," said one seasoned meal trader. "Too much cargo has arrived in too short a time, and people are just not wanting to accept it."
Earlier defaults were price driven, traders have said.

Following the Chicago Board of Trade's sharp drop in soymeal prices in mid-October, a rash of defaults on payments for meal and beans took place, triggering a flurry of negotiations between Chinese buyers and traders.
"Most of those should have cleared up already," another senior grains trader said.
The markets were said quiet on Wednesday, but price enquiries were still trickling in with interest still more in meal than in beans, traders said.
"People are just too nervous about the import restrictions next year," said one trader.
The market widely expects China to slap import restrictions on soybeans in 1997, but there have been no official announcements so far.
Nevertheless, one U.S soybean cargo was heard sold recently for delivery in early January, although the seller anticipated "problems" with the contract.
About 50,000 tonnes of Indian meal was heard sold to China for delivery in late December or early January.
The meal was sold at about $305 per tonne, C&F China, one industry source said.
A 10,000-tonne cargo of Indian meal was expected at Shanghai's port next week, and 9,000 tonnes of that had already been sold, a China-based source said.
Towards the end of December, another cargo of U.S. meal was expected in Shanghai, but no further details were available.
Domestic Chinese meal was 2,930 yuan ($353) per tonne.
Indian high protein was about 2,900 yuan ($349) per tonne, FOB Shanghai, compared to its price last month of about 2,950 yuan ($355) per tonne.
U.S. low protein (44 percent) was heard at about 2,850 yuan ($343) per tonne, FOB Shanghai.
